extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, scholars and theatre practitioners interested in Shakespeare's As You Like It
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting criteria and interpretive dimensions used to analyze, classify, stage, or historicize Shakespeare's play As You Like It. Includes thematic, stylistic, textual-historical, and performance-oriented aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral mode / pastoral comedy characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: "The main theme of pastoral comedy is love in all its guises in a rustic setting, the genuine love embodied by Rosalind contrasted with the sentimentalised affectations of Orlando, and the improbable happenings that set the urban courtiers wandering to find exile, solace or freedom in a woodland setting..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features to identify/expect when classifying or producing a pastoral comedy: a rustic/forest setting (Forest of Arden), love in varied forms, stock pastoral characters, light repartee, songs interrupting action, chance encounters rather than intricate plotting, and a final recovery of harmony (weddings, blessings). The page also notes Shakespeare 'develops' the genre to critique social practices that produce injustice and to satirize foolish/self-destructive behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prose and verse (dramatic convention defied)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Shakespeare used prose for about 55% of the text... The dramatic convention of the time required the courtly characters to use verse, and the country characters prose, but in As You Like It this convention is overturned."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a stylistic/evaluative criterion: examine who speaks prose vs verse and when characters switch modes. Examples given: Rosalind (a duke's daughter) often speaks in prose; Silvius describes his love in verse; the epilogue is prose; Jaques interrupts prose with a verse line. Use of prose/verse is a deliberate expressive tool for characterization and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: All the world's a stage / 'Seven Ages' monologue
rubrics_metrics.description: "Act II, Scene VII... features one of Shakespeare's most famous monologues, spoken by Jaques, which begins: 'All the world's a stage...'. The monologue describes a person's lifespan as a play in seven acts or 'ages'."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an interpretive criterion: analyze the monologue's philosophical framing of human life, its seven 'ages', and its recurrence as a thematic lens for the play's view of performance, identity, and social roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery of harmony (final reconciliation)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The ultimate recovery of harmony is marked with four weddings and a dance of harmony ... before most of the exiled court are able to return to the court and their previous stations are recovered."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating structure and thematic resolution, look for mechanisms of reconciliation (marriage, repentance, restoration of titles), symbolic rituals (Hymen's blessing, dance), and how disorder is transformed into social harmony by the play's end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court life vs country life (contrast theme)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The play begins in a courtly setting... Most of the play is then a celebration of life in the country, where after intensifying disorder, harmony is recovered. A passage between Touchstone, the court jester, and shepherd Corin establishes the contentment to be found in country life, compared with the perfumed, mannered life at court."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this binary as an evaluative axis: compare values, freedoms, dangers, and moral lessons attributed to court and country; note the inversion of expectations and how characters change by moving between settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love as central theme (varieties of love)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Love is the central theme of As You Like It... Love at first sight occurs between Rosalind and Orlando, Celia and Oliver, and Phebe and Ganymede. The love story of Audrey and Touchstone is a parody of romantic love. Another form of love occurs between women, as in Rosalind and Celia's deep bond."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how the play represents multiple forms of love (romantic, parody, friendship, unrequited), and how those forms are staged, parodied, or upheld. Consider how love interacts with social status, disguise, and reconciliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forgiveness and repentance (moral restoration)
rubrics_metrics.description: "These end happily with reconciliation and forgiveness. Duke Frederick is converted by a hermit and he restores the dukedom to Duke Senior... Oliver also undergoes a change of heart..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess character arcs for moral change, mechanisms prompting repentance (rescue, revelation, solitude), and the play's stance on restorative justice and forgiveness as dramatic resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Envy (motivating emotions and its dispelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article discusses envy as a theme and how the comedy provides respite from 'the envious court', with examples suggesting envy disappears with the appearance of the actor on stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use envy as an evaluative lens: identify scenes where jealousy/enmity drive conflict (e.g., Oliver's treatment of Orlando) and note symbolic or theatrical moments where envy is resolved or highlighted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender and cross-dressing (performance of gender)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The elaborate gender reversals in the story are of interest to modern gender studies. ... Rosalind, who in Shakespeare's day would have been played by a boy, finds it necessary to disguise herself as a boy... the rustic Phebe, also played by a boy, becomes infatuated with this 'Ganymede'."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or producing the play, focus on gender performance, role reversals, homoerotic overtones, metatheatrical complexity (actor playing boy playing girl playing boy), and scholarly debates about deconstruction vs re-entrenchment of gender roles. Note epilogue's explicit theatricality and modern queer readings mentioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious and mythological allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: "The play contains mythological references in particular to Eden and to Hercules."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate symbolism and allegory: how biblical and classical allusions (Eden, Hercules, Hymen) contribute to themes of innocence, trial, heroism, and marital ritual; use such references to frame moral or cultural readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music and songs integrated into action
rubrics_metrics.description: The article lists songs ('Under the Greenwood tree', 'Blow, blow, thou winter wind', 'It was a lover and his lass') and states these songs are incorporated in the action, summarise views, prelude the wedding, and announce rebirth of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat songs as functional dramaturgical elements: identify where songs comment on theme, set mood, announce transitions (seasonal, ritual), or are used for spectacle. Consider historical musical settings (Thomas Morley) and opportunities for adaptation (modern musical arrangements, folk/rock settings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting (Forest of Arden as symbolic and geographic construct)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Forest of Arden 'transcends singular identity and geography' and evokes Arcadia, the biblical garden of Eden, and possibly the French Ardennes or English Forest of Arden; the setting is both fantastical and symbolically resonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret setting both as literal location and as symbolic space (utopia/Arcadia/Eden) that permits social inversion, refuge, moral testing, and pastoral ideals. Consider production choices about which Arden (French Ardennes vs English Arden) to invoke and their implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source text and dating evidence (textual-historical criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: "As You Like It was first printed in the collected edition of Shakespeare's plays, known as the First Folio, during 1623. No copy of it in Quarto exists... By means of evidences, external and internal, the date of composition of the play has been approximately fixed at a period between the end of 1598 and the middle of 1599..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For textual-historical evaluation: use external evidence (Stationers' Register, musical settings like Morley's First Book of Ayres) and internal evidence (allusions to other works, topical references, anachronisms) to date and contextualize composition. Note limitations and uncertainty; cataloguing and Folio/Quarto status are relevant bibliographic criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance history and staging suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: The play has no certain record before the Restoration; notable modern productions are listed; 'The play ... has been found, by many directors, to be especially effective staged outdoors in a park or similar site.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning a production or assessing stagings, consider historical performance records, adaptability (period transposition, modern settings), suitability for outdoor site-specific performance, casting choices (including accessibility and diverse casting), musical adaptations, and critical reception of notable productions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stock characters, tone and comedic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The article emphasizes stock characters (the melancholy Jaques, the court jester Touchstone, shepherds, lovers) and notes 'the light repartee and the breadth of the subjects that provide opportunities for wit'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how stock types function in the play (comic foil, social commentary), the balance of wit/repartee vs melancholic reflection, and how comic devices (parody, pastoral parody, mock-marriage scenes) shape audience response and thematic meaning.
